title: Account registration data can identify the homeowner
description: During registration, the Home Hub receives identifiers such as name, email, phone number, home address, account credentials, and device identifiers. If collected or stored in a directly attributable form, this flow enables identification of the homeowner and household.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is my best-fit estimate for identifiability from directly identifying attributes; no reference tree was provided.

title: Enrollment links multiple devices and household activities to one account
description: Camera and sensor enrollment associates multiple devices, locations, and future event streams with a single homeowner account. This can create a rich linkable profile of the household across devices and rooms.
uncertainty_note: Node id is an estimated best fit for linkability through association of records/devices because no threat-tree reference was supplied.

title: Registration and device enrollment reveal household composition and setup
description: The kinds, number, names, and placement of enrolled cameras and sensors may disclose private facts about the home, such as occupancy patterns, room usage, security concerns, presence of children, or whether the property is vacant at times.
uncertainty_note: Node id is a best-effort estimate for disclosure of information in the transmitted enrollment metadata.

title: Homeowner may not understand the scope of enrollment data collection and downstream use
description: At account creation and device enrollment, the user may be unaware of what personal data the Home Hub collects, how long it is retained, whether video/sensor metadata is shared to cloud services, or what inferences can be drawn from the household setup.
uncertainty_note: Node id is my best-fit estimate for lack of awareness/transparency; exact LINDDUN Pro node may differ.

title: Registration and enrollment may collect more personal data than necessary
description: The flow may request or transmit excessive account details or detailed device metadata beyond what is needed to activate the Home Hub, conflicting with data minimization and privacy-by-default expectations.
uncertainty_note: Node id is an estimated best fit for non-compliance with data minimization/privacy-by-design obligations.

title: Insufficient proof of consent or enrollment actions could enable repudiation disputes
description: If the system does not keep privacy-respecting evidence that the homeowner accepted terms, consented to data processing where required, or initiated device enrollment, either party may later dispute what was agreed to or enrolled.
uncertainty_note: Best-fit node id for non-repudiation concerns; applicability depends on whether consent is the legal basis and what evidence is retained.

title: Observed registration timing or enrollment traffic can reveal user presence and behavior
description: Even if contents are protected, the fact that the homeowner is registering or adding devices at a specific time can reveal that someone is present at home, performing setup, or expanding monitoring coverage. Enrollment bursts may also reveal the scale of the installation.
uncertainty_note: Node id is a best-effort estimate for detectability via traffic/observable interaction patterns; no direct regulatory citation identified for this specific threat.

title: Observation of temporary access code entry can reveal household access patterns
description: A guest entering a temporary access code at the Home Hub may be observed by bystanders, cameras, or nearby attackers, allowing the code and the fact of a visit to be inferred. This can expose information about who is visiting the home and when, linking the guest to a specific household visit.
assumptions: The Home Hub is in a location where code entry may be visible or otherwise observable by unauthorized parties.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is best-effort from memory for information disclosure/observability; exact LINDDUN Pro node labeling may differ.

title: Temporary access code can act as a linkable identifier for guest visits
description: If the same temporary access code is reused across visits or logged together with time and device context, the Home Hub or associated systems may be able to link multiple access events to the same guest, building a profile of visits and associations with the household.
assumptions: Temporary codes may persist for more than one use or be stored in event logs with metadata.
uncertainty_note: Node id is approximate; threat is linkability through repeated or logged code use.

title: Temporary access code entry may identify the guest to the household or service
description: Where each temporary access code is uniquely assigned to a specific guest, entering the code identifies that guest to the Home Hub, household members, or backend services, potentially beyond what the guest expects when simply unlocking the front door.
assumptions: Each temporary code is unique per guest or invitation and is associated with an identifiable person in the system.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is uncertain; classification is identifiability arising from unique guest code assignment.

title: Guest may be unable to plausibly deny door unlock action
description: If the Home Hub logs successful code entry with timestamps and code identifiers, the guest may later be unable to deny having accessed the property at a particular time. This can create privacy risk if logs are retained, shared, or used in disputes.
assumptions: Access attempts and successful unlock events are logged and attributable to a specific temporary code.
uncertainty_note: Node id is best-effort for non-repudiation/accountability; exact LINDDUN Pro node may differ.

title: Guest may be unaware that code entry is logged or monitored
description: The guest may enter the temporary access code without clear notice that the Home Hub records access events, associates the code with their identity, or shares logs with household members or cloud services. This undermines user unawareness about collection and processing.
assumptions: The interface or invitation process does not clearly inform guests about logging, retention, sharing, or monitoring.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id is approximate; threat is user unawareness regarding collection and use of access data.

title: Collection and processing of guest access data may lack a valid legal basis or adequate notice
description: Processing temporary access codes and associated entry logs may constitute personal data processing if the code can be tied to a guest. If notice, consent, purpose limitation, retention limits, or other legal obligations are not met, the flow may create non-compliance risk.
assumptions: The system is subject to data protection law and temporary codes or logs can be related to an identifiable guest.
uncertainty_note: Citation is illustrative and jurisdiction-dependent; applicability depends on whether guest access logs are personal data and on deployment context.

title: Linkable in-home activity history in local event log
description: The local event log can accumulate timestamped motion, door, and sensor events that allow correlation across time, linking events to a household's routines, occupancy patterns, and potentially specific residents' behaviors.
assumptions: The log retains events over time and can be accessed by software, administrators, or someone with device access.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is a best-effort estimate from LINDDUN Pro taxonomy without reference material.

title: Identifiability of household members from sensor event patterns
description: Even if the log stores only sensor events, the pattern of door openings, motion triggers, and timing may identify a specific home or distinguish household members based on routine behavior.
assumptions: Event timestamps and sensor identifiers are stored with enough granularity to distinguish routines or individuals.
uncertainty_note: Node id is best-effort, and whether specific residents are identifiable depends on granularity and context.

title: Disclosure of occupancy and behavior from local event log
description: If the local log is read by unauthorized local users, malware, or service personnel, it may reveal when residents are home, asleep, away, or entering/exiting, exposing intimate household behavior.
assumptions: The data store is accessible locally or through maintenance/debug interfaces and contains readable event histories.
uncertainty_note: Best-effort node id without the threat tree reference.

title: Unawareness of persistent local logging of sensor events
description: Residents may not realize the Home Hub persistently writes motion, door, and sensor events to a local event log, including what is logged, for how long, and who can access it.
assumptions: The system does not clearly notify users about local event logging, retention, and access practices.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is approximate from memory.

title: Excessive or unjustified retention of local sensor event history
description: Persistently storing detailed home sensor events in the local log may exceed what is necessary for device operation or troubleshooting, conflicting with minimization and storage-limitation expectations.
assumptions: The log retains granular events beyond a short operational window or without a clear necessity.
uncertainty_note: This is framed as non-compliance risk based on likely minimization/retention issues; exact applicability depends on jurisdiction and product purpose.

title: Lack of proof or contestability for event-log writes
description: If the Home Hub writes events to the log without integrity protection or audit metadata, users may be unable to prove whether particular entries were created, altered, or deleted, undermining accountability for privacy-relevant logging.
assumptions: The system relies on the local log for later review, dispute handling, or incident analysis but does not protect provenance.
uncertainty_note: Node id is best-effort and applicability is somewhat context-dependent because non-repudiation threats are less central for simple local logging.

title: Detectability of presence through existence and timing of log entries
description: The mere presence, frequency, or timing of event-log entries can allow an observer to detect whether activity occurred in the home, even without reading full content, enabling inference of occupancy.
assumptions: An observer can determine that entries exist or monitor log growth, metadata, or indicators tied to the log.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is approximate without the official threat-tree list; regulatory citation is indirect.

title: Home Hub uploads identifiable video clips containing faces, voices, or household activity
description: Recorded camera clips can directly identify residents, visitors, or bystanders through facial images, voices, timestamps, and interior scenes when transmitted from the Home Hub to cloud storage.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is my best-fit estimate for identifiability of personal data in content; citation is general personal-data definition rather than a flow-specific obligation.

title: Cloud-stored clips may enable indirect identification through metadata and context
description: Even if video quality is reduced, associated metadata such as device identifiers, account linkage, upload times, location context, and recurring patterns can permit identification of a household or individual once stored in the cloud.
uncertainty_note: Node id is approximate for indirect identifiability via metadata/context.

title: Cloud storage can link multiple video clips to the same household or user account
description: Centralized cloud storage can associate uploaded clips over time with a persistent account, device, household, and camera, enabling profiling of routines, occupancy, visitors, and behavior across recordings.
uncertainty_note: Node id is best-fit for linkability across records; citation is approximate because purpose-limitation concerns arise when linked use extends beyond the original household-security purpose.

title: Presence, routines, and household activities are inferable from uploaded clips
description: The stored video clips can reveal when occupants are home, asleep, away, receiving visitors, or engaging in specific activities, allowing sensitive inferences about lifestyle and behavior.
uncertainty_note: Node id is an estimated inference-related node; citation is approximate because data minimization is implicated by collection of more information than necessary.

title: Special-category or highly sensitive information may be inferred from home video
description: Home camera footage may reveal health conditions, religious practices, children's presence, relationships, or other sensitive attributes from appearance, conversations, objects, or routines visible in the clips.
uncertainty_note: Node id is approximate for sensitive-attribute inference. Applicability of GDPR Art. 9(1) depends on actual content of the footage.

title: Uploading clips to cloud storage may occur without sufficient transparency to data subjects
description: Residents, visitors, domestic workers, or bystanders may not be aware that the Home Hub uploads recordings to remote cloud storage, how long they are retained, or who can access them.
uncertainty_note: Best-fit node for insufficient information/transparency; exact applicability depends on controller role and whether notice can practically be given to all captured individuals.

title: Individuals may lack meaningful control over cloud upload and retention of their images
description: People captured on camera may be unable to prevent upload, delete recordings, object to storage, or choose a local-only mode, undermining user and data-subject control over disclosure and retention.
uncertainty_note: Node id is an approximate best fit for lack of intervenability/unawareness of control. Erasure rights may not directly apply in every household-use scenario.

title: Cloud video storage may retain or reuse clips incompatibly with privacy principles
description: If uploaded clips are stored longer than necessary, reused for analytics or product improvement, or processed without a valid legal basis, the flow may violate purpose limitation, storage limitation, or lawfulness requirements.
uncertainty_note: Node id is approximate for policy/regulatory non-compliance. Additional provisions such as GDPR Art. 5(1)(b)-(e) and Art. 6 may also apply depending on service practices.

title: Sensitive occupancy inference from motion alert content
description: A real-time motion alert sent from the Home Hub to the backend can reveal that someone is currently present, active, or moving within the home. Repeated alerts may expose occupancy patterns, daily routines, sleep/wake times, or absences, making the event data privacy-sensitive beyond its operational purpose.
assumptions: Assumes the alert payload includes device, room, timestamp, or event metadata sufficient to infer household behavior.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is my best-fit estimate for inference from event data; exact LINDDUN Pro labeling may vary.

title: Linkability of motion events to a specific household or user account
description: When the backend receives motion alerts tied to a persistent hub identifier, account identifier, or network metadata, it may be possible to link multiple alerts to the same household over time. This enables profiling of behavior across sessions and devices.
assumptions: Assumes the backend stores persistent identifiers or metadata associated with the Home Hub or account.
uncertainty_note: Node id is a best-fit estimate for linkability via persistent identifiers.

title: Identifiability of residents from device and account metadata
description: Even if the motion event itself is not directly identifying, combining it at the backend with account records, device registration data, IP addresses, or location information can identify the household or specific residents associated with the alert.
assumptions: Assumes the backend has access to subscriber/account data or other identifying metadata.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is my best-fit estimate for direct or indirect identifiability through associated metadata.

title: Users may be unaware that raw motion events are transmitted to the backend in real time
description: Residents may not understand that in-home sensor activity is continuously or near-real-time forwarded from the Home Hub to the backend, potentially for alerting, analytics, retention, or secondary uses. This can undermine informed expectations and meaningful transparency.
assumptions: Assumes the service is subject to GDPR-like transparency obligations and that disclosures may be incomplete or unclear.
uncertainty_note: Citation depends on jurisdiction and whether the controller is subject to GDPR.

title: Collection and transmission of motion alerts may exceed data minimization or purpose expectations
description: Forwarding detailed, real-time motion alerts to the backend may collect more personal data than necessary if the same user-facing function could be achieved with less granular, less frequent, or more locally processed data. Secondary processing of these alerts may also be incompatible with the original purpose if not properly bounded.
assumptions: Assumes granular motion events are retained or further processed centrally rather than used ephemerally only for immediate notification.
uncertainty_note: This is a best-fit non-compliance mapping; data minimization under GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) may also apply.

title: Potential lack of lawful basis or valid consent for in-home monitoring data processing
description: Motion alerts from inside a home are highly privacy-relevant. If backend processing relies on consent or another lawful basis that is not properly established, documented, or scoped, the transmission and subsequent processing may be non-compliant.
assumptions: Assumes the deployment is in a jurisdiction requiring a lawful basis for processing personal data and that motion alerts qualify as personal data.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on jurisdiction and controller role; node id is a generic best-fit for compliance risk.

title: Excessive retention of motion alert history enables long-term profiling
description: If the backend stores transmitted motion alerts for extended periods, the retained history can reveal detailed long-term patterns about household occupancy, habits, vacations, and lifestyle. This increases privacy impact beyond the immediate alerting purpose.
assumptions: Assumes the backend persists event histories rather than discarding them quickly after alert delivery.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is my best-fit estimate for disclosure/detectability risks arising from stored event histories; exact LINDDUN Pro node naming may differ.

title: Notification content reveals occupancy or in-home activity to unintended viewers
description: A pushed motion-detected notification may be visible on the phone lock screen or notification tray and disclose that motion was detected at the home, revealing presence, absence, routines, or current activity to anyone who can see the device.
assumptions: Assumes notification text includes explicit motion/alert details rather than a generic app message, and that notifications can appear on a locked device.
uncertainty_note: LINDDUN Pro node id is my best fit for data disclosure via user-visible message content; exact subtree labeling may vary by catalog.

title: Push delivery and interaction patterns enable linkage of homeowner identity with home events
description: Repeated delivery of motion-alert notifications to a specific device/account can let the service provider or platform correlate the homeowner's identity, device token, and home event stream, linking surveillance events to a particular person or household over time.
assumptions: Assumes push notification identifiers or account identifiers are persistent and associated with the homeowner.
uncertainty_note: Tree node chosen as a best-fit linkage/correlation node; exact numbering may differ in some LINDDUN Pro versions. GDPR Art. 4(1) is definitional rather than an obligation, cited only because the flow can involve personal data.

title: Motion alerts can identify the homeowner's presence patterns and household behavior
description: Sending motion-detected notifications tied to a specific account can allow identification or singling out of the homeowner's daily routines, likely occupancy windows, or household behavior when combined with account and device information.
assumptions: Assumes the backend associates alerts with a named or otherwise attributable homeowner account.
uncertainty_note: Best-fit identifiability node selected from memory; citation is approximate and definitional.

title: Homeowner may be unaware of notification visibility and secondary use implications
description: The homeowner may not understand that motion-alert notifications can be displayed by the mobile OS, handled by third-party push providers, or retained in notification history, undermining informed expectations about how incident data is used and exposed.
assumptions: Assumes the service relies on standard mobile push infrastructure and presents notifications outside the app UI.
uncertainty_note: Node id is a best-effort fit for lack of awareness/transparency; exact LINDDUN Pro numbering may vary.

title: Push notification of home surveillance events may occur without valid consent or another clear lawful basis
description: If motion-detection alerts contain personal data about household activity or visitors, sending them via push infrastructure may be non-compliant where the app has not obtained valid consent for notifications, or has not otherwise established and communicated an appropriate lawful basis and purpose.
assumptions: Assumes motion alerts constitute personal data processing and that notification permissions / privacy choices may be insufficiently captured or documented.
uncertainty_note: This is a broad compliance threat; exact applicability depends on jurisdiction and whether another lawful basis besides consent is used. Tree node is best-effort.

title: Insufficient evidence of notification delivery or user review can create repudiation issues around privacy events
description: If the system cannot demonstrate what notification content was sent, when it was sent, and whether the homeowner viewed it, parties may later dispute whether a sensitive alert was disclosed or acted upon, complicating privacy incident handling and user rights requests.
assumptions: Assumes logging/audit trails for outbound notifications are limited or not integrity-protected.
uncertainty_note: Repudiation is a weaker fit for this flow than disclosure/unawareness; included with lower confidence. Node id is approximate.

title: Backend can disclose linkable analytics records to vendor
description: Even if the shared analytics are described as aggregated, combinations of device-usage dimensions, timestamps, app version, region, and cohort attributes may allow the cloud analytics vendor to link repeated submissions to the same user segment, household, or device over time. This can enable cross-dataset correlation and re-identification of ostensibly aggregate analytics.
assumptions: Assumes the aggregation level may still leave small cells or stable cohort identifiers, and the vendor receives data frequently enough to correlate reports over time.
uncertainty_note: LINDDUN Pro node id is my best-fit estimate for linkability on this flow; exact node naming may vary by catalog edition. Citation is approximate because whether data are 'personal data' depends on actual aggregation and re-identification risk.

title: Vendor can infer user or household behavior from aggregated usage analytics
description: The cloud analytics vendor may infer sensitive characteristics or behavioral patterns from aggregate device-usage analytics, such as sleep/activity rhythms, presence patterns, feature adoption by demographic segment, or likely household composition, especially when combined with the vendor's existing datasets.
assumptions: Assumes analytics include sufficiently granular dimensions or cohorts from which sensitive traits or special-category inferences could be derived.
uncertainty_note: Node id is a best-fit estimate for inferability. GDPR Art. 9(1) may apply only if special-category data or equivalent inferences are realistically derivable; otherwise a more general GDPR citation would be more appropriate.

title: Sharing analytics with third-party vendor may exceed user expectations or declared purpose
description: Users may not expect device-usage analytics collected to operate or improve the mobile service to be disclosed to an external analytics vendor for separate analysis, benchmarking, or product improvement. If notices do not clearly explain this transfer and its purposes, the disclosure can undermine transparency.
assumptions: Assumes the vendor is a separate recipient and the app's privacy notice may not fully disclose the categories of recipients and purposes of transfer.
uncertainty_note: Best-fit detectability/disclosure-related node id; exact LINDDUN Pro numbering may differ.

title: Users may lack meaningful awareness or consent choice for analytics sharing
description: If the mobile app backend sends analytics to the cloud analytics vendor without a clear opt-in/opt-out mechanism or layered notice, users may be unaware of the transfer or unable to exercise meaningful choice, especially where analytics are not strictly necessary for service delivery.
assumptions: Assumes consent is the chosen lawful basis or that local law/policy requires a user choice for non-essential analytics sharing.
uncertainty_note: Node id is a best-fit estimate for unawareness/unintervenability. Citation is conditional because another lawful basis besides consent may be claimed.

title: Transfer to analytics vendor may be incompatible with purpose limitation or data minimization obligations
description: Sending aggregated device-usage analytics to an external vendor can create non-compliance risk if the transfer is broader than necessary, retains unnecessary dimensions, or is reused for purposes incompatible with the original collection context. Aggregation alone does not eliminate compliance duties if the dataset remains attributable or reasonably re-identifiable.
assumptions: Assumes the shared analytics may still fall within privacy law scope and are subject to purpose limitation/minimization requirements.
uncertainty_note: Best-fit non-compliance node id. Additional or alternative citations such as GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) or Art. 28 could also be relevant depending on controller/processor roles.

title: Vendor processing may not be sufficiently attributable or auditable
description: If the analytics vendor receives aggregate usage data without strong contractual logging, provenance, and processing records, it may be difficult to later prove what data were received, what transformations were applied, or whether onward use stayed within agreed purposes. This impairs accountability for privacy-relevant actions on the flow.
assumptions: Assumes limited audit logging, data lineage, or processor accountability controls for the vendor relationship.
uncertainty_note: LINDDUN node id is a best-fit estimate for non-repudiation/accountability gaps; catalog wording may differ. GDPR Art. 5(2) is a broad accountability citation rather than a flow-specific duty.

title: Unauthorized backend retrieval of stored video clip
description: If the mobile app backend retrieves a video clip from cloud storage without strong authorization checks tied to the requesting homeowner, video footage may be disclosed to another user, an over-privileged service, or an attacker abusing backend access.
assumptions: Stored clips can contain personal data about residents, visitors, or bystanders, and backend retrieval is triggered on behalf of an authenticated user.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is best-effort based on general LINDDUN knowledge; citation is approximate because no jurisdiction or regulatory scope was specified.

title: Backend can infer sensitive household behavior from playback requests
description: By retrieving specific stored clips for playback, the backend may infer occupancy patterns, routines, visitor presence, or incident-related activity associated with the homeowner account, beyond what is necessary to serve the request.
assumptions: Playback requests are logged or otherwise observable by the backend and linked to an identifiable account.
uncertainty_note: Node id is a best-effort estimate; inference applicability depends on logging, analytics, and retention practices not described in the prompt.

title: Retrieval events are linkable to a specific homeowner account across sessions
description: Repeated backend retrievals of stored clips can be linked to the same account, device, or household over time, enabling construction of a detailed viewing history associated with an identifiable person or home.
assumptions: The backend maintains stable identifiers or logs that connect retrieval events over time.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is best-effort from general LINDDUN knowledge; citation is approximate because applicability depends on whether such secondary use occurs.

title: Insufficient evidence of user-initiated retrieval or administrative access
description: If retrieval of stored video clips is not logged with sufficient integrity and context, the system may be unable to prove whether a clip was accessed by the homeowner, by support staff, or by an unauthorized actor, undermining accountability for privacy-relevant disclosures.
assumptions: Multiple actors or services may be able to trigger clip retrieval, and audit trails are necessary for accountability.
uncertainty_note: LINDDUN node id is best-effort; GDPR accountability citation is approximate and may not map directly to a single flow-level threat.

title: Excessive video data returned to backend
description: Cloud storage may provide more video data than necessary for the requested playback, such as extended time ranges, extra camera segments, or unnecessary metadata, resulting in needless exposure of personal data to the backend.
assumptions: Storage retrieval interfaces may support broad object access or bundled metadata beyond the minimum needed to fulfill playback.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is best-effort and may be more specific in a full LINDDUN Pro catalog.

title: Users may be unaware that backend access to clips occurs during playback
description: Homeowners may assume video playback is a direct client-to-storage action, while in reality the backend retrieves and can potentially inspect or log the clip, reducing transparency about who accesses footage and for what purpose.
assumptions: The system architecture and privacy notice do not clearly explain backend-mediated retrieval and associated processing.
uncertainty_note: Node id and citation are best-effort; transparency obligations depend on controller role and the actual notices provided.

title: Retrieval processing may exceed declared purpose or lawful basis
description: Using backend-mediated retrieval data for analytics, model training, employee monitoring, or other secondary purposes beyond providing playback could violate purpose limitation or fail to match the user's consent or other lawful basis.
assumptions: The backend or surrounding services may reuse clip content or retrieval metadata for secondary processing.
uncertainty_note: This threat depends on downstream use not described in the prompt; node id is best-effort from general LINDDUN knowledge.
